# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Review of "Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations"

This is a useful follow-up. It addresses the open questions from the earlier papers:
- **Durability:** it uses a 24-month horizon.
- **Measurement:** it adds log-based hours alongside timesheets.
- **Mechanism:** it runs a registered mediation test.
- **Decay:** it checks the meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies. They were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, as suspected.
- **Counter arm:** it reports the arm's termination plainly.

Most of its responses to the earlier claims are fair. Four things deserve more attention:
- control offices cut their own meetings, which contaminates the comparison;
- it is unclear what the log measure counts, which affects how the mediation result should be read;
- the mediation inference is less independent and less precise than it appears;
- the 24-month Halden figures are framed as an upper bound when they are not one.

## Arithmetic check

Most figures are consistent:
- Per-hour gain, timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 = **+9.8%** ✓
- Per-hour gain, logs: 0.966 / 0.89 = **+8.5%** ✓
- Halden hours: 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 (−13.4%) ✓
- Halden per-hour gain: 0.968 / 0.866 = **+11.8%** ✓
- Mediation shares: 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 ✓
- Meeting time, difference-in-differences: −3.5 h (treated) vs −0.2 h (control), a difference of 3.3 h ✓

Two descriptions don't match the numbers:
- **"Declined by about a quarter"** (§5). On the like-for-like timesheet measure, 12.5% → 9.8% is a fall of about **a fifth** (22%). "A quarter" falls between this and the 32% you'd get comparing 12.5% (timesheets) with 8.5% (logs), which mixes measures.
- **"Log data show slightly more work than timesheets."** The table shows *percentage changes*: −11% on logs, −12% on timesheets. That says hours fell slightly less on logs. It says nothing about which measure records more work in absolute terms. Report the levels.

## 1. Control offices cut their own meetings during the trial

The two control offices that ran a "meeting audit" in month 15 are presented as an interesting side observation. They also contaminate the comparison:
- **The 24-month estimate may be biased downward.** If cutting meetings raises output per hour, which is the paper's own mediation finding, then two of seven control offices improved partway through. That narrows the treatment–control gap for months 15–24.
- **The "fading" could partly be control improvement.** Some of the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may come from control offices getting better, not treated offices getting worse. The paper attributes the decline to fading without considering this.
- **The other control offices' meeting time appears to have risen.** Average control meeting time is 7.0 h at month 24. Two offices were at 5.0 h. So the other five must average about **7.8 h**, up from roughly 7.2 h at baseline. This may be a timing artefact if 5.0 h is a six-month average and 7.0 h a point value, but it should be explained.

The paper should report:
- the 24-month estimates excluding the two auditing offices;
- treatment–control gaps for months 10–15 and 16–24 separately, before and after the audit.

## 2. What do the system logs measure?

The logs record "active log-in time on the county's case-management system… time staff are working on cases". If that is literal, the logs mostly exclude meetings, training and other non-case work. That has two consequences:
- **Logs are not a stricter version of total hours.** They measure casework time, a different quantity. Output per log-hour is output per hour of casework, not per hour worked. Both are informative, but the paper treats logs as a more accurate total.
- **The mediation result is hard to interpret.** If meeting time is outside the denominator, cutting meetings cannot raise output per log-hour through the obvious route, which is moving time from meetings to cases. A 47% mediation share on this outcome would then mean meetings affect the *speed* of casework, through less fragmentation or fewer interruptions. That is a different and more interesting claim. Alternatively, staff stay logged in during meetings, in which case the logs aren't measuring casework.

The paper should state:
- what the logs capture, including whether time in meetings or idle logged-in time counts;
- whether pre-period log data exist. The log-based figures carry no 9-month value, and "hours fell 11%" needs a baseline. If logs only exist from later in the trial, the log-based difference-in-differences needs explaining.

## 3. The mediation analysis

The registered test is a real improvement on the 9-month correlation. Its framing overstates it in three ways:
- **It isn't independent confirmation.** The hypothesis came from the same seven treated offices it is now tested on. Registering at month 11 prevents choosing the model after seeing the outcome. It does not make the data independent of the data that generated the hypothesis. "Survives a registered test" is accurate. "Confirms" in the Summary is too strong.
- **Office-months are not independent.** Treatment and most of the variation in meetings occur at office level, so the effective sample is 14 clusters, 7 treated. A CI of 28%–66% on a mediation share seems narrow for that. Specify how clustering was handled and whether small-cluster corrections were applied, such as a wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference.
- **There is confounding between mediator and outcome.** The limitations note this, and it applies directly. Managers who cut meetings most may also be the ones who reorganise work in other ways. Then "meetings" stands in for "management response to the hours cut".

A fair summary: the registered analysis is consistent with meetings being an important pathway, and the estimate is imprecise and drawn from the same offices. Independent replication is needed.

### The control-office observation, read quantitatively

As a rough check: 47% of 8.5% is about 4.0 percentage points, from 3.3 h of meeting reduction. That is about 1.2 points per hour cut. At that rate, the two control offices' 2.1-hour cut predicts about 2.5%. They gained **4.1%**, more than predicted.

Several factors argue against reading much into this:
- it is two offices with no comparison group;
- offices that audit themselves may have done so after a weak period, so regression to the mean is possible;
- if these offices were contaminating the control arm, as argued in §1, they cannot also serve as clean evidence.

The paper's own caution here is appropriate.

## 4. The counter arm's staffing estimate

The county estimated that restoring service needs **12% more staff**, at **+9% cost per contact**. This probably understates the cost:
- **Arithmetic.** Actual hours fell about 17%. Restoring presence with no productivity change would need about 1/0.83 ≈ **20% more staff**. The 12% figure implies the 6.7% per-hour gain persists: 1/(0.83 × 1.067) ≈ 1.13.
- **Why the gain won't persist.** In coverage-bound work, that per-hour gain most likely came from higher utilisation: fewer staff serving the same queue with less idle time. Restoring short waits means restoring idle capacity, which removes the gain. The true requirement is likely closer to 20% than 12%.

The cost-per-contact figure should be recalculated on that basis, or the assumption stated.

Separately, the termination is a useful result in its own right, and reporting it plainly is to the paper's credit. In months 10–12, waits were 7.3 minutes in treated offices against 4.0 in control. This is the first treatment-vs-control waiting-time comparison in the series.

## 5. The Halden 24-month subset

- **"Upper bound" is the wrong frame.** Selection pushes the estimate up: survivors twice over, and only 14 of 23 organisations responded. But a two-year uncontrolled before–after comparison also absorbs everything else that changed between 2023 and 2025: the economy, staffing, and the spread of productivity tools, including generative AI in marketing and professional services. Those could push the figure in either direction. Better wording: "biased upward by selection and confounded by two years of secular change; not an estimate of a causal effect."
- **Non-response.** 9 of 23 organisations did not respond. If non-responders were more likely to have reverted, the reversion rate (3 of 14) is understated. Describe the non-responders, if anything is known about them.
- **The reverters don't all fit the coverage story.** The Summary says all three reverters had "client-facing or coverage obligations". One is a **marketing agency citing client deadlines**. That is deadline-driven, discretionary work by the meta-analysis's coding, not coverage-bound. Grouping it under "coverage obligations" hides a case that cuts against the paper's dichotomy. Deadline-driven client work may be a third category worth naming.
- **Output at reversion.** Indices of 88–91 at the time of reversion support the earlier finding that customer-facing settings lose output. They also show that reverters were not marginal cases.

## 6. The responses to earlier claims

- **On the re-analysis.** The rebuttal is fair on substance. Varden at 24 months meets the standards the re-analysis recommended: records, actual hours, randomisation, at least 18 months' follow-up, and all enrolled units analysed. It still finds a gain. Two qualifications:
  - The re-analysis extrapolated *self-reported energy* to baseline, not output. Its own arithmetic gave about month 8.7, not ten. Saying the gain did not "fall to zero by month ten" argues against a slightly stronger claim than was made, though the substantive point stands.
  - The 24-month estimate may be biased downward by control contamination (§1), so it is if anything conservative. That strengthens the rebuttal.
- **On the meta-analysis.** This is the paper's most valuable correction. If the four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, the "no decay" conclusion can't stand. However, the 9-month and 24-month CIs overlap heavily (6.9–18.4 vs 4.6–15.2). Report a formal test of the change. A within-office estimate of the difference will be more precise than comparing the two intervals.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Conflict of interest.** R. Okafor, an author of the original Halden working paper, co-authors a follow-up that re-analyses Halden organisations and responds to a critique of Halden. The Varden authors are likewise responding to critiques of their own work. This is normal, but it should be declared.
- **Missing uncertainty.** Appeal overturn rates and resignations still have no CIs. The 24-month overturn rate is welcome, because appeals have now had time to resolve.
- **Sick days.** The −27% still includes the mechanical effect of fewer scheduled days, if the 30-hour week is worked as four days. Report sickness per scheduled day.
- **What was ruled out.** "No arm reorganised without reducing hours" is exactly right. The obvious next study is a three-arm trial: reduced hours, reorganisation alone (such as a meeting audit), and control.

## Where the series now stands

Taking all five documents together:

| Question | Best current evidence |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain in discretionary work | Roughly **8–10%**, persisting at 24 months in one randomised trial, possibly declining. Smaller than the 20%+ of early pilots. |
| Output per employee, discretionary work | Slightly below control: about −2% to −3%, CIs including zero. |
| Coverage-bound work | Output per employee falls about 9–11%. Waits rise. The per-hour gain is probably a utilisation effect. The one randomised arm was ended. |
| Mechanism | Meeting reduction is plausibly a major contributor and fatigue a smaller one. Estimates are imprecise, come from a single trial, and the meaning depends on what the logs measure. |
| Novelty | Some decline from 9 to 24 months, possibly overstated by control contamination. No evidence the gain disappears. |
| Can the gain be had without cutting hours? | Untested. It needs a reorganisation-only arm. |

Overall: the per-hour gain in discretionary work is real but modest, it costs some output per employee, and it does not carry over to coverage-bound work. How much of it comes from the hours cut itself, rather than the reorganisation the cut prompts, is still unknown.
